observation.visible_scene: Nighttime elevated (likely drone) view over a large open paved plaza. A multi-story building under construction with a tower crane sits on the left; a dense crowd of spectators lines the bottom foreground; distant streetlights and city glow fill the background. In the center of the plaza a fireworks display is actively running, with sky bursts above and ground-level flares/fountains at the launch area.
visible_changes: Repeated bright white flashes erupt at the center of the display, each expanding into a large glowing burst surrounded by smoke (e.g., early frames, and again around the middle and later frames).
Colored aerial shells burst and fade in sequence: red/white starbursts appear, then green bursts, then white/gold chrysanthemum-type bursts higher in the sky, each expanding outward and dimming.
Ground-level pyrotechnic flares change color and intensity over time, shifting among green, red, and finally sustained orange/red fountains that shoot upward from several points on the plaza floor.
Smoke from the explosions accumulates and drifts upward and to the right, partially obscuring the sky and the building across the sequence.
The crowd and the building remain stationary throughout; the visible motion is expansion of bursts and rising smoke, not translation of scene objects.
Several frames appear washed-out/overexposed (pinkish haze) coinciding with the brightest flashes, consistent with camera auto-exposure reacting to intense light rather than a change in the scene.
outside_clip_unknowns: How the display was initiated and what controls each shell or flare.
Whether the sequence continues to a finale or stops after the last frame.
Exact launch mechanics and operator positions, which are hidden by smoke and distance.
uncertain_details: Camera is presumed to be a static hover; minor framing differences could be jitter but background alignment suggests little intentional movement.
True colors of some bursts are hard to judge because bright flashes blow out the exposure.
Individual crowd members and small ground objects are too distant/obscured to track.
